key_terms.meaning: A P-T (or P-V-T) map of a pure substance showing solid, liquid and gas regions and the lines where two phases coexist
The single temperature and pressure where solid, liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium; for water 273.16 K and 611.657 Pa
The highest temperature and pressure at which a liquid and its vapour can be told apart; above it only a supercritical fluid exists
The pressure at which a liquid and its vapour coexist at a given temperature; it rises with temperature and ends at the critical point
PV = nRT, where P is pressure (Pa), V volume (m³), n moles (mol), T absolute temperature (K) and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)
A path at constant temperature; for an ideal gas ΔU = 0 and the work done by the gas is W = nRT ln(V<sub>2</sub>/V<sub>1</sub>) = Q
A path with no heat transfer (Q = 0); for a reversible ideal-gas path PV<sup>γ</sup> = constant with γ = C<sub>p</sub>/C<sub>v</sub>
A path with PV<sup>k</sup> = constant; k = 0 isobaric, k = 1 isothermal, k = γ adiabatic, k → ∞ isochoric
Z = 1 + B/V + C/V² + … or Z = 1 + B′P + C′P² + …; B is the second virial coefficient and carries the first correction for molecular interaction
(P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT with V the molar volume; b is the excluded volume and a/V² the attraction correction

key_terms.term: van der Waals constants from critical data
key_terms.meaning: a = 27R²Tc²/(64Pc) and b = RTc/(8Pc); the predicted Zc = 3/8 = 0.375 against about 0.27 for real fluids
P = RT/(V − b) − a(T)/[(V + εb)(V + σb)] with a = Ψα(T<sub>r</sub>)R²T<sub>c</sub>²/P<sub>c</sub> and b = ΩRT<sub>c</sub>/P<sub>c</sub>; van der Waals, RK, SRK and PR differ only in ε, σ, Ω, Ψ and α
Z = PV/RT per mole; Z = 1 for an ideal gas, below 1 when attraction dominates and above 1 when molecular size dominates
Tr = T/Tc, Pr = P/Pc, Vr = V/Vc; dimensionless variables that make different fluids fall on common curves
Fluids at the same T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub> have about the same Z; with the acentric factor as a third parameter, Z = Z⁰ + ωZ¹
ω = −1.0 − log<sub>10</sub>(P<sub>r</sub><sup>sat</sup>) at T<sub>r</sub> = 0.7; it measures how far a molecule departs from a simple spherical fluid
Z = 1 + (B⁰ + ωB¹)P<sub>r</sub>/T<sub>r</sub>, B⁰ = 0.083 − 0.422/T<sub>r</sub><sup>1.6</sup>, B¹ = 0.139 − 0.172/T<sub>r</sub><sup>4.2</sup>; for low to moderate P<sub>r</sub>
Heat that changes the temperature of a single phase: Q = n∫C<sub>p</sub> dT from T<sub>1</sub> to T<sub>2</sub>, or n C̄<sub>p</sub> ΔT with a mean C<sub>p</sub>
Heat absorbed or released at constant temperature during a phase change, such as ΔHvap at the boiling point
ΔH°rxn = Σνᵢ ΔH°f,i for products minus reactants, both at 298.15 K and 1 bar
d(ΔH°<sub>rxn</sub>)/dT = ΔC<sub>p</sub> = Σν<sub>i</sub>C<sub>p,i</sub> (ν positive for products, negative for reactants); it shifts a heat of reaction to another temperature
ΔHvap, the heat to convert one mole of saturated liquid to saturated vapour at the same temperature and pressure; it falls to zero at the critical point

takeaways: A pure fluid in one phase is fixed by two intensive variables, on a phase boundary by one, and at the triple point by none; the phase diagram shows which case applies.
The ideal gas law is a limiting law at low pressure and high temperature; it fails whenever molecules are close together.
Each ideal-gas path (isothermal, adiabatic, isochoric, isobaric, polytropic) has its own work and heat relations; state the sign convention before using them.
The virial equation is a systematic correction that gets better as more coefficients are added; the van der Waals equation is a simple closed-form model that predicts a critical point.
The compressibility factor Z can be read from a generalized chart or computed from the Pitzer virial correlation or a generalized cubic, using only T<sub>r</sub>, P<sub>r</sub> and ω.
Real-gas behaviour is well organized: attraction makes Z < 1 at moderate pressure, size makes Z > 1 at high pressure, and fluids with the same ω sit on a common curve.
Heat effects come in three kinds — sensible, latent and chemical — and each has its own calculation route.
Kirchhoff's equation is what lets you take a table value at 298 K and use it at your reactor temperature.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit ask you to write an equation with every symbol and unit, derive or justify it (van der Waals constants, the phase rule, corresponding states), and then use it in a numerical part. Show the reduced conditions before any generalized correlation, and say whether the method is inside its range.

bank.q: State the ideal gas law and define the compressibility factor Z. List the two physical assumptions behind the ideal gas model and say which one fails first at high pressure.
outline: PV = nRT with P in Pa, V in m³, n in mol, T in K, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)
Z = PV/(nRT), equal to 1 for an ideal gas
Assumptions: molecules have negligible volume, and no forces between them except collisions
At moderate pressure attraction shows first and Z falls below 1; at high pressure molecular size wins and Z rises above 1
Low-pressure slope (b − a/RT)/RT: negative below the Boyle temperature
answer: State the law. PV = nRT, with P the absolute pressure (Pa), V the volume (m³), n the amount (mol), T the absolute temperature (K) and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) = 0.08314 L·bar/(mol·K). Per mole, PV = RT with V the molar volume.

Define Z. The compressibility factor Z = PV/(nRT) = PV/RT per mole. It is the ratio of the real molar volume to the ideal-gas molar volume at the same T and P, so Z = 1 for an ideal gas at every T and P, Z < 1 when the real gas takes less room and Z > 1 when it takes more.

The two assumptions. (1) The molecules are points: their own volume is negligible next to the volume of the container. (2) There are no forces between molecules except elastic collisions: no attraction, no repulsion at a distance. Together they make U and H functions of T only.

answer.text: Which fails first. At low pressure both assumptions hold and Z → 1. Raising the pressure brings molecules close enough to feel their attraction long before they are packed tightly, so for most gases at ordinary temperatures attraction shows first and Z falls below 1. Only at high pressure does the volume of the molecules dominate and push Z above 1. The van der Waals low-pressure form shows this:
answer.pre:
Z ≈ 1 + (b − a/RT) P/RT
CO₂, a = 3.640 L²·bar/mol², b = 0.04267 L/mol, T = 300 K:
b − a/RT = 0.04267 − 3.640/24.942 = −0.1033 L/mol  → Z < 1
at 40 bar: van der Waals Z = 0.801 (the molecules take 20 % less room)

answer: Boyle temperature. The attraction term shrinks as T rises. When b = a/RT, the two effects cancel at low pressure: T<sub>B</sub> = a/(Rb) = 3.640/(0.08314 × 0.04267) = 1026 K for van der Waals CO₂. Above T<sub>B</sub> the size effect wins at every pressure and Z > 1 throughout (hydrogen and helium at room temperature are already above their Boyle temperatures).

Conclusion. The no-attraction assumption fails first, at moderate pressure, giving Z < 1; the point-molecule assumption fails at high pressure, giving Z > 1. Use PV = nRT only when Z is within about 1 to 2 % of 1, which for most gases means a few bar or less.

bank.q: Draw the P-T phase diagram of a pure substance and explain each region and each line. Mark the triple point and the critical point, and explain what happens on heating at constant pressure (a) below the triple-point pressure, (b) between the triple-point and critical pressures, (c) above the critical pressure.
outline: Axes P (y) and T (x); regions solid, liquid, vapour
Sublimation, fusion and vaporisation curves meeting at the triple point
The vaporisation curve ends at the critical point
Below P<sub>t</sub>: heating crosses only the sublimation curve
Between P<sub>t</sub> and P<sub>c</sub>: melting, then boiling
Above P<sub>c</sub>: melting, then a continuous change to a supercritical fluid with no boiling
answer: Draw the diagram. Pressure on the vertical axis (a log scale helps), temperature on the horizontal. Three single-phase regions: solid at high P and low T, liquid in the middle, vapour at low P and high T. Three lines separate them; along each line two phases coexist, so a point on a line is a two-phase state with F = 1.

answer.text: Name the lines and the special points (values for water).

head: Feature
Separates
Water
rows: almost vertical, leans left (ice melts when squeezed)
from the triple point to the critical point; 1.01325 bar at 100.0 °C

answer: Phase rule. F = C − π + 2 with C = 1 component and π phases: one phase F = 2 (choose T and P freely), on a line F = 1 (choosing T fixes P), at the triple point F = 0 (one state only).

(a) Heating below the triple-point pressure, for water at 0.005 bar. Starting from ice at −40 °C, the horizontal line meets only the sublimation curve, at about −2 °C: ice turns straight into vapour (as frost vanishes on a freeze-drier shelf) and the liquid never appears.

(b) Heating between the triple-point and critical pressures, for water at 1 bar. Ice warms to 0 °C and melts at constant temperature (fusion curve); the liquid warms to 99.6 °C and boils at constant temperature (vaporisation curve) with a latent heat; the vapour then superheats. Two plateaus on a heating curve.

(c) Heating above the critical pressure, for water at 250 bar. Ice melts on the fusion curve, but the line passes above the critical point, so it never meets the vaporisation curve. The liquid turns gradually into a supercritical fluid: density falls steadily, no meniscus forms, no bubbles appear and there is no latent heat.

At the critical point itself the saturated liquid and saturated vapour have the same density, the latent heat falls to zero and the meniscus disappears. Above T<sub>c</sub> no pressure, however high, can liquefy the fluid.

bank.q: Write the van der Waals equation and explain the physical meaning of the constants a and b. Show how the critical-point conditions (∂P/∂V)T = 0 and (∂²P/∂V²)T = 0 lead to a = 27R²Tc²/(64Pc) and b = RTc/(8Pc).
outline: P = RT/(V − b) − a/V² written in P form
b corrects volume for molecular size; a/V² corrects pressure for attraction
Set (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = 0 and (∂²P/∂V²)<sub>T</sub> = 0 at the critical point
Solve with the equation itself: V<sub>c</sub> = 3b, T<sub>c</sub> = 8a/(27Rb), P<sub>c</sub> = a/(27b²)
Invert to a and b in terms of T<sub>c</sub>, P<sub>c</sub>
Z<sub>c</sub> = 3/8 against 0.23 to 0.29 for real fluids

answer.text: Write the equation per mole (V is the molar volume).
answer.pre: (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT     or     P = RT/(V − b) − a/V²

answer: Meaning of b. Molecules have a finite size, so the space free for their motion is less than V. b is the excluded volume per mole, about four times the volume of the molecules themselves; it raises the pressure above the ideal value at a given V.

Meaning of a. Molecules attract each other. A molecule about to hit the wall is pulled back by its neighbours, so it strikes with less force. The loss depends on the number of pairs, proportional to (1/V)², so the correction is a/V². It lowers the pressure.

answer.text: Critical conditions. The critical isotherm has a horizontal inflection at the critical point, so both derivatives vanish there:
answer.pre:
(∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub>   = −RT/(V − b)² + 2a/V³ = 0   →  RT/(V − b)² = 2a/V³      (1)
(∂²P/∂V²)<sub>T</sub> = 2RT/(V − b)³ − 6a/V⁴ = 0  →  RT/(V − b)³ = 3a/V⁴      (2)

answer.text: Solve. Divide (1) by (2), then substitute back.
answer.pre:
(V − b) = 2V/3          →  V<sub>c</sub> = 3b
(1): RT<sub>c</sub> = 2a(2b)²/(3b)³ = 8a/(27b)   →  T<sub>c</sub> = 8a/(27Rb)
P<sub>c</sub> = RT<sub>c</sub>/(2b) − a/(9b²) = 4a/(27b²) − 3a/(27b²) = a/(27b²)

answer.text: Express a and b through the measured T<sub>c</sub> and P<sub>c</sub> (V<sub>c</sub> is hard to measure, so it is not used).
Numbers for CO₂ (T<sub>c</sub> = 304.2 K, P<sub>c</sub> = 73.8 bar, R = 0.08314 L·bar/(mol·K)).

answer: Consequence. Z<sub>c</sub> = P<sub>c</sub>V<sub>c</sub>/RT<sub>c</sub> = [a/(27b²)](3b)/[8a/(27b)] = 3/8 = 0.375 for every van der Waals fluid. Real fluids have Z<sub>c</sub> between about 0.23 and 0.29 (CO₂ 0.274), so van der Waals predicts too large a critical volume and is poor near the critical point and for liquids.

bank.q: Explain the principle of corresponding states. Define Tr, Pr and the acentric factor, and state why a third parameter improves the correlation.
outline: T<sub>r</sub> = T/T<sub>c</sub>, P<sub>r</sub> = P/P<sub>c</sub>; Z plotted against P<sub>r</sub> with T<sub>r</sub> as parameter
Two-parameter statement: fluids at the same T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub> have the same Z
Acentric factor ω = −1.0 − log<sub>10</sub>(P<sub>r</sub><sup>sat</sup>) at T<sub>r</sub> = 0.7
Simple spherical molecules (Ar, Kr, CH₄) have ω near 0; larger or polar molecules have larger ω
Third parameter separates the families of curves: Z = Z⁰ + ωZ¹
answer: Reduced properties. T<sub>r</sub> = T/T<sub>c</sub>, P<sub>r</sub> = P/P<sub>c</sub>, V<sub>r</sub> = V/V<sub>c</sub>, all dimensionless. They measure how far a state is from that fluid's own critical point.

Two-parameter principle of corresponding states. All fluids at the same T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub> have about the same Z. Its basis is the reduced van der Waals equation, (P<sub>r</sub> + 3/V<sub>r</sub>²)(3V<sub>r</sub> − 1) = 8T<sub>r</sub>, which contains no constant of any particular gas. One chart of Z against P<sub>r</sub>, with a curve for each T<sub>r</sub>, then serves every gas once T<sub>c</sub> and P<sub>c</sub> are known.

Why it is not enough. The principle works well for simple spherical molecules (argon, krypton, xenon, methane), but non-spherical and polar molecules fall on different curves: at the same T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub>, n-butane and argon do not have the same Z. The clearest sign is the reduced vapour pressure: at T<sub>r</sub> = 0.7, simple fluids all have P<sub>r</sub><sup>sat</sup> ≈ 0.1, while others have less.

answer.text: Acentric factor (Pitzer). It measures that difference:
answer.pre:
ω = −1.0 − log<sub>10</sub>(P<sub>r</sub><sup>sat</sup>) at T<sub>r</sub> = 0.7
simple fluid: P<sub>r</sub><sup>sat</sup> = 0.1  → ω = 0
n-butane:     ω = 0.200 → P<sub>r</sub><sup>sat</sup> = 10<sup>−1.2</sup> = 0.0631 (37 % lower)
water:        ω = 0.345

answer.text: Three-parameter correlation. Z = Z⁰ + ωZ¹, where Z⁰ (simple fluid) and Z¹ (correction) are tabulated against T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub>. At low pressure the same idea gives the Pitzer virial form. Compare a simple fluid with n-butane at T<sub>r</sub> = 1.1997, P<sub>r</sub> = 0.6586 (510 K, 25 bar):

answer: Why the third parameter helps. With ω the single family of curves becomes a family for each ω, and errors fall from several per cent to one or two per cent for normal fluids. It still fails for strongly polar or hydrogen-bonding fluids (water, ammonia, alcohols) and for quantum gases (hydrogen, helium), which need extra parameters or special equations of state.

bank.q: One mole of an ideal gas at 300 K is compressed reversibly and isothermally from 1 bar to 10 bar. Calculate w, q, ΔU and ΔH, and state the sign convention used.
outline: Convention: W is work done by the gas, ΔU = Q − W
Isothermal ideal gas: ΔU = 0 and ΔH = 0
W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁) = nRT ln(P₁/P₂)
n = 1 mol, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), T = 300 K, P₁/P₂ = 0.1
W = −5743 J (work done on the gas)
Q = W = −5743 J: heat leaves the gas
answer: Convention. W is the work done by the gas and Q the heat added to it, so ΔU = Q − W. Compression therefore has W < 0.
State functions. For an ideal gas U and H depend on T only. T is constant, so ΔU = 0 and ΔH = 0.

answer.text: Volumes, for the record.
Work. Reversible, so P = nRT/V along the path:

answer: Heat. Q = ΔU + W = 0 + (−5743.1) = −5743.1 J. The 5.743 kJ of work done on the gas leaves it as heat to the surroundings; that is what keeps the temperature at 300 K.

answer.text: Summary.

answer: In the chemistry convention (w = work done on the gas, ΔU = q + w) the same process has w = +5743 J and q = −5743 J; always state which convention you use.

bank.q: One mole of an ideal gas with Cp = 29.1 J/(mol·K) and Cv = 20.8 J/(mol·K) is compressed reversibly and adiabatically from 1 bar and 300 K to 5 bar. Find the final temperature and the work.
outline: T₂ = T₁ (P₂/P₁)<sup>(γ−1)/γ</sup>
ΔU = n C<sub>v</sub> (T₂ − T₁) = 3635 J; Q = 0
W by the gas = −ΔU = −3635 J
answer: Data and convention. n = 1 mol, C<sub>p</sub> = 29.1 and C<sub>v</sub> = 20.8 J/(mol·K), P₁ = 1 bar, T₁ = 300 K, P₂ = 5 bar. W is work done by the gas; ΔU = Q − W. Check: C<sub>p</sub> − C<sub>v</sub> = 8.3 J/(mol·K) ≈ R, as it must be for an ideal gas.

answer.text: Heat-capacity ratio.
Final temperature. A reversible adiabatic path of an ideal gas follows TP<sup>(1−γ)/γ</sup> = constant:
Energy terms.
answer.pre:
Q = 0                                     (adiabatic)
ΔU = n C<sub>v</sub> (T₂ − T₁) = 20.8 × 174.77 = 3635.2 J
W = Q − ΔU = −3635.2 J                     (work done on the gas)
ΔH = n C<sub>p</sub> (T₂ − T₁) = 29.1 × 174.77 = 5085.8 J

answer.text: Check through volumes.

answer: Answer. T₂ = 474.8 K and the work done on the gas is 3.64 kJ (W = −3635 J by the gas). An isothermal compression over the same pressure ratio would need 4014 J (W = −RT ln 5 at 300 K), because it squeezes the gas to a smaller final volume, 4.99 L against 7.89 L.

bank.q: Carbon dioxide has Tc = 304.2 K and Pc = 73.8 bar. Using the van der Waals equation, estimate the pressure exerted by 1 mol of CO₂ in a 0.5 L vessel at 300 K, and compare it with the ideal gas value.
outline: Work in L, bar and K with R = 0.08314 L·bar/(mol·K), or in SI
a = 27R²T<sub>c</sub>²/(64P<sub>c</sub>) = 3.657 L²·bar/mol², b = RT<sub>c</sub>/(8P<sub>c</sub>) = 0.04284 L/mol
Ideal gas P = RT/V = 49.88 bar
Z = 0.80: attraction dominates; the ideal gas is 25 % high
answer: Data. T<sub>c</sub> = 304.2 K, P<sub>c</sub> = 73.8 bar, T = 300 K, n = 1 mol, V = 0.5 L, so the molar volume is 0.5 L/mol. Use R = 0.08314 L·bar/(mol·K), so that P comes out in bar.

answer.text: Constants from the critical point.
van der Waals pressure.
Ideal gas and comparison.

answer: Interpret. The size term alone would raise the pressure to 54.6 bar, 9 % above ideal, but attraction removes 14.6 bar, so the real pressure is 20 % below ideal. At this density (about 2 mol/L) attraction dominates, as expected for CO₂ just below its critical temperature. The ideal gas law is not acceptable here; van der Waals is a fair first estimate, and a modern cubic (Peng–Robinson) should be used for design.

bank.q: A gas has Tc = 400 K, Pc = 40 bar and ω = 0.2. Estimate its molar volume at 500 K and 20 bar using the generalized compressibility chart or the Pitzer correlation.
outline: T<sub>r</sub> = 500/400 = 1.25, P<sub>r</sub> = 20/40 = 0.5: inside the Pitzer virial range
Z = 1 + (B⁰ + ωB¹)P<sub>r</sub>/T<sub>r</sub> = 0.921
V = ZRT/P with T in K and P in Pa
V = 1.914 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m³/mol

answer.text: Reduced conditions.

answer: Choose the method. At T<sub>r</sub> = 1.25 and P<sub>r</sub> = 0.5 the reduced volume is well above 2, where Z is nearly linear in pressure, so the Pitzer virial correlation applies and no chart reading is needed.

answer.text: Generalized virial coefficients.
Compressibility factor.
Molar volume, in SI units.

answer: Answer. Z = 0.921 and V = 1.91 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m³/mol, 8 % below the ideal-gas value. The ω term changes Z by only 0.006 here; it matters more at lower T<sub>r</sub> and higher P<sub>r</sub>.

bank.q: Calculate the heat needed to raise 2 mol/s of nitrogen from 300 K to 700 K at 1 bar, using Cp = 31.15 − 0.01357(T/K) + 2.68×10⁻⁵(T/K)² − 1.17×10⁻⁸(T/K)³ J/(mol·K).
outline: Sensible heat at constant pressure: Q = n∫Cp dT
Integrate each term between 300 K and 700 K
Multiply by 2 mol/s and state the answer in W or kW
Note the assumption of ideal-gas Cp and no phase change
Mention that the same integral gives ΔH
answer: Set up. Constant pressure, no phase change, ideal-gas heat capacity: the heat equals the enthalpy rise, Q̇ = ṅ∫C<sub>p</sub> dT from 300 K to 700 K, with ṅ = 2 mol/s.

answer.text: Integrate term by term (C<sub>p</sub> = α + βT + γT² + δT³).
answer.pre: ∫C<sub>p</sub> dT = α(T₂ − T₁) + (β/2)(T₂² − T₁²) + (γ/3)(T₂³ − T₁³) + (δ/4)(T₂⁴ − T₁⁴)

answer.text: Numbers, T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 700 K.
Heat rate.

answer: Check. The mean heat capacity is 11 890.3/400 = 29.73 J/(mol·K), between C<sub>p</sub>(300 K) = 29.18 and C<sub>p</sub>(700 K) = 30.77 J/(mol·K), as it must be. Using the 300 K value throughout would give 23.3 kW, 2 % low.

Assumptions and note. Nitrogen at 1 bar behaves as an ideal gas, so C<sub>p</sub> is the ideal-gas value and H does not depend on pressure; there is no phase change. The same integral is ΔH of the nitrogen, the quantity used in any steady-flow heater balance (Q̇ = ṅΔH with no shaft work).

bank.q: Liquid water at 373 K and 1 atm is fully vaporized. Using ΔHvap = 40.66 kJ/mol at 373 K, find the heat needed per kg of water, and explain why the temperature stays constant during vaporization.
outline: Moles per kg = 1000/18.015 = 55.5 mol
Latent heat goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not kinetic energy
Therefore temperature is constant until all liquid disappears
Link to the enthalpy change of vaporization in steam tables

answer.text: Heat per kilogram.

answer: Check. Steam tables give h<sub>fg</sub> = 2256.4 kJ/kg at 100 °C, so the molar value reproduces the table within 0.03 %. At constant pressure the heat supplied equals the enthalpy change, which is why ΔH<sub>vap</sub> is the latent heat.

answer.text: Split of the latent heat. Part of it pushes back the atmosphere as the vapour forms:

answer: Why the temperature stays constant. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules. During boiling the energy goes into pulling molecules apart against their attraction (hydrogen bonds in water), which raises their potential energy, plus the PΔV work. With liquid and vapour both present at fixed pressure the phase rule leaves F = 1, so fixing P = 1 atm fixes T at 100 °C until the last liquid disappears.

Link to tables. Steam tables list h<sub>f</sub>, h<sub>g</sub> and h<sub>fg</sub> = h<sub>g</sub> − h<sub>f</sub> at each saturation temperature; h<sub>fg</sub> falls as T rises and reaches zero at the critical point.

bank.q: Liquid water at 1 bar and 298 K is heated to 1 bar and 400 K. Sketch the path on a temperature–enthalpy plot and calculate ΔH per mole using sensible heat plus latent heat.
outline: Path: heat liquid to 373 K, vaporise at 373 K, superheat vapour to 400 K
ΔH = ∫C<sub>p,liq</sub> dT + ΔH<sub>vap</sub> + ∫C<sub>p,vap</sub> dT
C<sub>p,liq</sub> ≈ 75.3, C<sub>p,vap</sub> ≈ 33.6 J/(mol·K), ΔH<sub>vap</sub> = 40.66 kJ/mol
ΔH ≈ 47.2 kJ/mol; steam tables give about 47.3 kJ/mol
answer: Path. Because H is a state function, any path between the end states gives the same ΔH; choose one that uses known data. (1) Heat the liquid from 298 K to the boiling point, (2) vaporise at the boiling point, (3) superheat the vapour to 400 K. At exactly 1 bar water boils at 372.8 K; the 373 K value of ΔH<sub>vap</sub> is used, which changes the result by well under 0.1 %.

Sketch. On a T–H plot: a sloping line from 298 K up to 373 K (sensible heat of the liquid), a long horizontal step at 373 K (latent heat), then a short sloping line up to 400 K (sensible heat of the vapour, which takes less than half the heat per kelvin of the liquid).

answer.text: Data and steps (per mole).
Per kilogram.

answer: Check against steam tables. h(1 bar, 400 K) − h(liquid, 298 K) is about 2730 − 105 = 2625 kJ/kg, or 47.3 kJ/mol: within 0.2 % of the step-by-step value. Latent heat is 86 % of the total; forgetting the superheat step would cost only 2 %, but forgetting the latent heat would cost 86 %.

bank.q: Plot and compare Z against P at fixed T for (a) an ideal gas, (b) a gas following the truncated virial equation Z = 1 + BP/RT, and (c) a van der Waals gas. Explain the low-pressure limit in each case and show why the virial and van der Waals curves start with the same slope.
outline: All three start at Z = 1 as P → 0
Ideal: Z = 1, slope 0
Truncated virial: straight line of slope B/RT
van der Waals at low P: Z ≈ 1 + (b − a/RT)P/RT, so B = b − a/RT and the slopes match
Below the Boyle temperature the slope is negative; above it, positive
Truncated virial fails at high density; van der Waals loops near condensation
answer: Low-pressure limit. As P → 0 the molecules are far apart, neither size nor attraction matters, and every model gives Z → 1.
(a) Ideal gas: Z = 1 at every pressure, a horizontal line of slope 0.
(b) Truncated virial: Z = 1 + BP/RT, a straight line through Z = 1 with slope dZ/dP = B/RT. It bends nowhere, so it can only follow a real isotherm over the range where that is nearly straight.

answer.text: (c) van der Waals. Write Z = PV/RT = V/(V − b) − a/(RTV) and expand for large V:
answer.pre:
Z = 1/(1 − b/V) − a/(RTV) ≈ 1 + (b − a/RT)/V + b²/V² + …
with 1/V ≈ P/RT at low pressure:
Z ≈ 1 + (b − a/RT) P/RT     →  B<sub>vdW</sub> = b − a/RT

answer: Same slope. The second virial coefficient of a van der Waals gas is B = b − a/RT, so at P → 0 the van der Waals curve leaves Z = 1 with exactly the slope of the truncated virial line, (b − a/RT)/RT. Both describe the same physics at low density: pairs of molecules, with size (b) pushing Z up and attraction (a/RT) pulling it down.

answer.text: Numbers for CO₂ at 300 K (a = 3.640 L²·bar/mol², b = 0.04267 L/mol): B = 0.04267 − 3.640/24.942 = −0.1033 L/mol, slope −0.00414 per bar.

answer: Temperature effect. The slope is negative while a/RT > b, that is below the Boyle temperature T<sub>B</sub> = a/(Rb) = 1026 K for this CO₂; Z dips below 1 before rising at high pressure. Above T<sub>B</sub> (at 1200 K, B = +0.0062 L/mol) Z rises from the start. Sketch: three curves leaving Z = 1 at P = 0, the ideal flat, the virial a straight falling line, the van der Waals curve falling with it and then bending up.

Which to trust. Ideal gas: only near P = 0. Truncated virial: to moderate density (V<sub>r</sub> above about 2, a few tens of bar for CO₂ at 300 K); it already differs by 0.03 at 40 bar. van der Waals: qualitatively right at all densities, but below T<sub>c</sub> it loops through the two-phase region and needs the Maxwell construction, and its numbers are poor near the critical point.

bank.q: A pipeline carries natural gas, taken as pure methane, at 150 bar and 300 K (T<sub>c</sub> = 190.6 K, P<sub>c</sub> = 45.99 bar, ω = 0.012). Compare the ideal gas, van der Waals and generalized (Pitzer and cubic) routes for the molar volume used to size the pipe, and recommend one for plant design, giving reasons.
outline: T<sub>r</sub> = 1.574, P<sub>r</sub> = 3.262: high reduced pressure
Ideal gas V = RT/P = 0.1663 L/mol
van der Waals Z = 0.785; SRK 0.851; Peng–Robinson 0.805
Pitzer virial is outside its range (V<sub>r</sub> about 1.4)
The ideal gas overstates the volume by 17 to 27 %
Recommend Peng–Robinson or SRK, checked against measured data; cost and safety of a wrong volume

answer.text: Reduced state.
van der Waals from the critical constants.
answer.pre:
a = 27R²T<sub>c</sub>²/(64P<sub>c</sub>) = 2.303 L²·bar/mol²,  b = RT<sub>c</sub>/(8P<sub>c</sub>) = 0.04307 L/mol
solve P = RT/(V − b) − a/V² for V at 150 bar:  V = 0.1305 L/mol, Z = 0.785

answer.text: Generalized cubics in reduced form, Z = 1 + β − qβ(Z − β)/[(Z + εβ)(Z + σβ)], iterated from Z = 1.

answer: Pitzer virial correlation. It would give Z = 0.752, but at P<sub>r</sub> = 3.3 the reduced volume is only about 1.4, far below the V<sub>r</sub> ≥ 2 where Z is linear in P. The answer must not be used; the Lee–Kesler chart (Z = Z⁰ + ωZ¹) is the generalized route at this pressure.

answer.text: Compare.

head: Route
Z
Effort
Verdict at 150 bar
rows: right direction, poor accuracy at high P<sub>r</sub>

answer: Consequence for the pipe. For a fixed molar flow the volumetric flow, and so the velocity and pressure drop, scale with Z. Sizing with the ideal gas would overstate the gas volume by 1/0.805 − 1 = 24 % against Peng–Robinson: a larger, dearer pipe, wrong compressor duty and wrong line-pack (the gas stored in the line), which also sets how much gas escapes in a rupture. Underestimating Z the other way would undersize the line and raise velocities and erosion.

Recommendation. Use a cubic equation of state (Peng–Robinson or SRK) with the real gas composition and mixing rules, as process simulators do; natural gas is not pure methane, and CO₂, ethane and nitrogen change Z by several per cent. Because PR and SRK themselves differ by about 6 % here, check the chosen model against measured densities or a reference equation for natural gas before final design, and keep a design margin. Use the ideal gas only for a first order-of-magnitude estimate.

bank.q: The standard heat of a reaction is tabulated at 298.15 K. Explain how you would find the adiabatic reaction temperature of an industrial reactor operating at 700 K, and discuss which heat effects you must include.
outline: Use Kirchhoff's equation to shift ΔH°rxn to 700 K
Energy balance: heat released by reaction = sensible heat to raise products to T<sub>ad</sub>
Include any latent heats if a phase change occurs
Include excess reactants and inerts in the Cp sum
Iterate on T<sub>ad</sub> since Cp values depend on temperature
Discuss why actual reactor temperature is lower — heat losses, incomplete conversion, side reactions
answer: Definition. The adiabatic reaction temperature is the temperature the products reach when the reaction runs with no heat loss and no work: all the heat released stays in the product stream. It is the highest temperature the reactor can reach and sets materials, catalyst life and whether cooling is needed.

Use the state-function path. Enthalpy does not depend on the path, so split the real process (feed at T<sub>in</sub> → products at T<sub>ad</sub>) into (1) the reaction at the feed temperature, then (2) heating all products, inerts and leftover reactants from T<sub>in</sub> to T<sub>ad</sub>. The energy balance is ΔH<sub>1</sub> + ΔH<sub>2</sub> = 0.

answer.text: Shift ΔH°<sub>rxn</sub> from 298.15 K to the feed temperature with Kirchhoff's law. Ammonia synthesis, N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, feed at 700 K (C<sub>p</sub> taken constant: NH₃ 35.06, N₂ 29.12, H₂ 28.82 J/(mol·K)):
Energy balance. Basis: 1 mol N₂ + 3 mol H₂ fed at 700 K, 15 % of the N₂ converted (extent ξ = 0.15 mol).

answer: Heat effects to include. (1) The heat of reaction at the right temperature (Kirchhoff). (2) Sensible heat of every species leaving: products, unconverted reactants and inerts, since inerts and excess reactants absorb heat and lower T<sub>ad</sub>. (3) Latent heat if any species condenses or evaporates on the way (water in a combustor leaves as vapour, so the lower heating value applies). (4) Side reactions with their own heats. (5) The extent actually reached: equilibrium limits conversion, and for an exothermic reaction the limit falls as the temperature rises.

Iteration. C<sub>p</sub> rises with temperature, so with polynomial C<sub>p</sub> data the sensible-heat integral is nonlinear in T<sub>ad</sub>: guess T<sub>ad</sub>, evaluate the mean C<sub>p</sub> between T<sub>in</sub> and the guess, solve for a new T<sub>ad</sub>, and repeat until it stops changing. If conversion depends on temperature, the energy balance and the equilibrium relation are solved together.

Why the real reactor runs cooler. Heat leaks through walls, conversion is incomplete or limited by equilibrium, inerts dilute the feed, and endothermic side reactions take heat. The adiabatic value is therefore an upper bound used for safety and design, while the actual outlet temperature comes from the full balance with losses.

bank.q: Relate the shape of a van der Waals P-V isotherm below Tc to the phase behaviour of a real fluid. Explain the Maxwell equal-area construction and why the experimental path is flat.
outline: Below T<sub>c</sub> the van der Waals isotherm has a minimum and a maximum (a loop)
Between them (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub> > 0: unstable; between the spinodal and the saturation points: metastable
Maxwell: horizontal line at P<sub>sat</sub> with equal areas above and below
CO₂ at 280 K: P<sub>sat</sub> = 52.83 bar, V<sub>l</sub> = 0.0809, V<sub>g</sub> = 0.2655 L/mol
Real fluid: liquid and vapour coexist at constant P while V changes
Above T<sub>c</sub> the loop vanishes; at T<sub>c</sub> it shrinks to the inflection point
answer: Shape below T<sub>c</sub>. Below the critical temperature a van der Waals isotherm, followed from large V to small V, rises, reaches a local maximum, falls to a local minimum, then rises steeply on the liquid side: an S-shaped loop. Between the maximum and the minimum (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub> > 0, so squeezing the fluid would lower its pressure; such states are mechanically unstable and never observed.

Real behaviour. A real fluid compressed at constant T condenses at a single pressure, the vapour pressure: the isotherm is flat between the saturated-vapour volume V<sub>g</sub> and the saturated-liquid volume V<sub>l</sub>, and the system is a mixture of the two. The loop parts between the saturation points and the extrema are metastable: supersaturated vapour and superheated liquid, which can exist briefly in very clean systems (cloud chambers, bumping in boiling).

answer.text: Maxwell equal-area construction. At equilibrium the two phases have equal Gibbs energy. Along an isotherm dG = V dP, so ∫V dP over the loop from V<sub>l</sub> to V<sub>g</sub> must be zero. That is the same as requiring the horizontal line at P<sub>sat</sub> to cut equal areas from the loop:
answer.pre:
∫ P dV (from V<sub>l</sub> to V<sub>g</sub>, along the loop) = P<sub>sat</sub>(V<sub>g</sub> − V<sub>l</sub>)
van der Waals:  RT ln[(V<sub>g</sub> − b)/(V<sub>l</sub> − b)] + a(1/V<sub>g</sub> − 1/V<sub>l</sub>) = P<sub>sat</sub>(V<sub>g</sub> − V<sub>l</sub>)
with P<sub>sat</sub> = P(V<sub>l</sub>) = P(V<sub>g</sub>) from the equation itself

answer.text: Worked for CO₂ at 280 K (a = 3.640 L²·bar/mol², b = 0.04267 L/mol). Guess P<sub>sat</sub> between the loop's minimum and maximum, find the outer roots of the cubic, check the areas, and adjust until they match:

svg.aria: The van der Waals isotherm of carbon dioxide at 280 kelvin between 0.05 and 0.4 litres per mole, with a loop dipping to 41.5 bar and rising to 57.2 bar. A horizontal line at 52.83 bar runs from the liquid volume 0.0809 to the vapour volume 0.2655 and cuts the loop into two shaded areas of equal size.

answer: How good is it. van der Waals puts P<sub>sat</sub> of CO₂ at 280 K at 52.8 bar; the measured value is about 42 bar, so the equation overpredicts by roughly a quarter. Modern cubics (SRK, PR) with the ω-dependent α(T<sub>r</sub>) are fitted to vapour pressures and do much better; the equal-area idea is the same and is how they compute VLE.

Approach to the critical point. As T rises the maximum and minimum move together and the two-phase line shortens. At T<sub>c</sub> (304.0 K for these constants) they merge into a single inflection with (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = 0 and (∂²P/∂V²)<sub>T</sub> = 0, at V<sub>c</sub> = 3b = 0.128 L/mol and P<sub>c</sub> = a/(27b²) = 74.0 bar: exactly the conditions used to find a and b. Above T<sub>c</sub> the isotherm falls monotonically, there is one root at every pressure, and no phase split.

glossary.def: ω = −1.0 − log<sub>10</sub>(P<sub>r</sub><sup>sat</sup>) at T<sub>r</sub> = 0.7; zero for simple spherical molecules, 0.200 for n-butane.
The final temperature reached when the heat of reaction is entirely absorbed by the products, with no heat loss.
The temperature at which the second virial coefficient is zero, so a gas stays nearly ideal over a range of low pressures; a/(Rb) for a van der Waals gas.
The vapour pressure at the critical temperature, the highest pressure at which liquid and vapour can coexist.
The temperature above which a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone.
An equation of state that is cubic in molar volume, such as the van der Waals, Redlich-Kwong or Peng-Robinson equation.
The number of intensive variables that can be fixed independently; for a pure fluid F = 3 − π: two in one phase, one on a phase boundary, zero at the triple point.
H = U + PV, a state function convenient for constant-pressure processes.
A graph of Z against Pr with lines of constant Tr, allowing Z to be read for any gas.
The heat needed to raise one mole by one kelvin at constant pressure; Cp = (∂H/∂T)P.
The heat needed to raise one mole by one kelvin at constant volume; Cv = (∂U/∂T)V.
A property that does not depend on the amount of material, such as P or T.
The energy stored in the molecules of a system, excluding bulk kinetic and potential energy.
A path at constant pressure; for an ideal gas Q = ΔH and the work done by the gas is W = PΔV.
A path at constant volume; no P–V work is done, so W = 0 and Q = ΔU.
κ = −(1/V)(∂V/∂P)<sub>T</sub>, how much volume shrinks as pressure rises; about 4.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup> bar<sup>−1</sup> for liquid water at 25 °C.

Pseudo-critical constants of a mixture as mole-fraction averages, T<sub>pc</sub> = Σy<sub>i</sub>T<sub>c,i</sub> and P<sub>pc</sub> = Σy<sub>i</sub>P<sub>c,i</sub>; rough when the components differ much.
The vapour pressure from a cubic equation below T<sub>c</sub> is the horizontal line that cuts equal areas from the loop of the isotherm.
A substance made of one chemical species, so its state needs only two independent intensive variables.
The difference between a real-fluid property and its ideal-gas value at the same T and P; generalized correlations give it from T<sub>r</sub>, P<sub>r</sub> and ω.
A path through a series of equilibrium states; between the same two end states it gives the most work in an expansion and needs the least in a compression.
The condition where two phases coexist at equilibrium at a given T and P.
The pure substance at 1 bar and a stated temperature, usually 298.15 K, used as the reference for heats of formation.
A tabulated set of properties of water and steam, organized by saturation pressure or temperature and by superheat.
A fluid above both Tc and Pc, with properties between those of a liquid and a gas.
A coefficient in the virial series; the second virial coefficient B carries the correction for pairs of molecules interacting.
β = (1/V)(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>, how fast volume grows with temperature; about 2.6 × 10<sup>−4</sup> K<sup>−1</sup> for liquid water at 25 °C.
